name: CortiSlim
lead: CortiSlim is a branded dietary supplement that was marketed in the 2000s as a 'cortisol control' weight-loss formula, aimed at people who wanted to lose belly fat and slim down. It was sold by CortiSlim International and originally by Window Rock Enterprises, and it combined several herbal blends including magnolia bark, green tea extract and banana leaf extract.[1]

The marketing idea was that stress raises cortisol and that cortisol promotes fat storage, particularly around the abdomen, so a product that managed cortisol would help the user get leaner. Its three blends were presented as handling cortisol (Cortiplex), appetite and metabolism (Leptiplex), and blood sugar (Insutrol).[1]

The US Federal Trade Commission took action against the original marketer for false advertising, and the line was acquired in 2008.[1] No independent clinical trials of CortiSlim itself were found, and the product features in T Nation forum threads from 2003 to 2007 mostly as an example of heavily advertised diet pills.[2][3][4]

chain: Supplement marketed to lower stress-driven cortisol
Claimed less abdominal fat storage and appetite
angle.text: CortiSlim was sold to people wanting a leaner look, especially around the waist, through the idea that stress hormones drive fat gain. The claimed route was cortisol control plus appetite and blood-sugar support.

infobox: Magnolia bark, L-theanine, green tea extract, bitter orange, banana leaf extract, vanadyl sulfate
FTC false-advertising action; original owner went bankrupt

paras: The product contained three proprietary blends plus vitamin C, calcium and chromium. Cortiplex contained magnolia bark extract, beta-sitosterol and L-theanine and was promoted for managing cortisol and reducing abdominal fat. Leptiplex contained green tea leaf extract and bitter orange peel extract (synephrine) and was promoted for appetite control, energy and metabolism. Insutrol contained banana leaf extract and vanadyl sulfate and was promoted for blood sugar and insulin balance.[1]
Under a settlement, the current owner no longer describes CortiSlim as a cortisol antagonist.[1]

Window Rock Enterprises, the original marketer, lost a false-advertising case brought by the FTC and went into bankruptcy; the CortiSlim line was acquired in 2008.[1] The FTC found false the promoters' claim that more than 15 years of scientific research demonstrated the products' effectiveness.[1]

The Wikipedia article states a $12 million fine in 2007, but notes that its cited sources conflict on the amount and date, with one source headlined with a $25 million figure.[1] A 2007 T Nation post reproduces text reporting that the FTC fined the makers of TrimSpa, Xenadrine EFX, CortiSlim and One-A-Day WeightSmart for similar claims.[2]

timeline.event: FTC action against the original marketer over cortisol and weight-loss claims; reports differ on the fine.[1][2]
CortiSlim line acquired from bankrupt Window Rock Enterprises.[1]

lore.intro: On T Nation between 2003 and 2007, CortiSlim comes up in threads on cortisol and fat loss, in questions about diet pills, and in members' comments on its advertising slogan.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: Controlling stress-related cortisol lets you lose fat without diet or exercise
claims.believers: The product's advertising was summarised by forum members as saying fat gain is caused by stress rather than by the user; one member asks other T Nation members for input on CortiSlim and TrimSpa for his wife.[4][5]
claims.experts: The FTC found false the promoters' claim of more than 15 years of research supporting the products, and no independent trial of the product was found.[1]

claims.claim: Cortisol from stress and training can be offset with a supplement
claims.believers: Several T Nation members invoke CortiSlim in threads about cortisol and training stress, often with irony about the marketing.[3][5]
claims.experts: No published study has tested CortiSlim's blends as a combination for cortisol or body-fat outcomes.

card.summary: A cortisol-themed diet supplement whose advertising drew an FTC false-advertising action and which has no published trials behind it.
card.note: Research claims in its advertising were found false by the FTC.

quick.overview:
CortiSlim is a brand of weight-loss supplements marketed around lowering the stress hormone cortisol. It combines herbal blends including magnolia bark, green tea and banana leaf extracts.

The FTC found its claims of supporting research to be false, and no independent clinical trials were found.
quick.mechanism: The marketing proposed that blends could modulate cortisol, appetite and blood sugar. No studies were found showing the product changes cortisol or body weight.
quick.risks: Ingredients include bitter orange (synephrine), green tea extract and vanadyl sulfate, whose safety profiles are discussed elsewhere in the literature. The product's marketing was the subject of FTC action and the original marketer went bankrupt.
